newsitem.title: GERMANY: German government denies Kohl plans early tax cuts.
newsitem.headline: German government denies Kohl plans early tax cuts.

text.p: The German government denied on Sunday Chancellor Helmut Kohl was planning to bring forward a tax-cutting package to improve his chances of winning a record fifth term in office.

A report in the Welt am Sonntag weekly said the chancellor had told economic policy specialists in his Christian Democratic Union (CDU) earlier this month the party would need to go into the 1998 general having reduced the tax burden.
Kohl's centre-right coalition is committed to a major tax reform, expected to include a hefty cut in the top rate of income tax and attempts to simplify the complicated system.

The chancellor's liberal coalition partners, the Free Democrats (FDP), want the changes to begin in 1998. But the CDU has so far backed Finance Minister Theo Waigel, who says such a comprehensive reform could not be put in place before 1999.

Government spokesman Peter Hausmann inisted the government's plans had not changed. "Reports that the chancellor is planning a significant reduction in the tax burden for 1998 are wrong," he said in a statement.
A commission, chaired by Waigel, charged with formulating the plans is expected to present its conclusions soon.
"The plan remains to wait until the middle of December and discuss within the coalition how to proceed with tax policy in the light of the tax commission's conclusions," Hausmann said.
Welt am Sonntag said Kohl had warned that going into the elections without any tax cuts would play into the hands of the FDP and opposition Social Democrats (SPD).
"We mustn't be crazy and go into the general election without any tax reductions while the SPD and FDP are demanding massive cuts," the paper quoted him as saying.
It said he had also cited his political role model, Konrad Adenauer, Germany's first postwar chancellor.
"It was Adenauer who said: You only win elections through people's wallets'," Kohl reportedly said.

CDU members approved the broad outline of the tax reform at their party congress in Hanover last month and their Bavarian sister party, Waigel's Christian Social Union, followed suit at their conference in Munich on Saturday.

Under the proposals, the top tax income rate would drop from 53 to around 35 percent and the lowest rate would fall from 25.9 to under 20 percent. To finance the changes, a myriad of complicated tax breaks would be abolished.
FDP leader Wolfang Gerhardt vowed his party would continue to press within the coalition for at least some parts of the reform to be introduced before the next election.
"We want some elements to take effect at the beginning of 1998," he said in a weekend interview.
He pointed out one way to reduce the tax burden would be a sizeable cut in the hated "solidarity surcharge" on income tax, imposed to help pay for the costs of German unification.
Plans to cut the surcharge were postponed last month to plug gaps in next year's budget. The coalition has agreed it will be reduced later but has not specified the size of the cut.
